propositions.text: The Appellant, a Chinese citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of China, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying her claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal.
propositions.quote: She has not submitted new evidence in support of her appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant asks the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find her a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, or refer back for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection or, in the alternative, refer her claim back to the RPD for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant, a Chinese citizen, appeals the RPD decision denying refugee protection without new evidence and asks the RAD to set aside or refer back the decision.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), the RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA s.111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Appellant alleged fear of persecution in China due to activities and membership in the XXXX Christian underground house church in Guangxi.
propositions.quote: The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she fears persecution in China on the basis of her activities and membership in the XXXX sect of the Christian underground house church in Guangxi province.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleged fear of persecution in China due to her activities and membership in the underground Christian house church.

propositions.text: The RPD heard the claim on Nov 19, 2015 and rejected it on Dec 17, 2015, finding the Appellant not credible on central elements.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's claim for refugee protection was heard on November 19, 2015. In a decision of December 17, 2015, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim finding that the Appellant was not credible about the central elements of her claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD heard the claim in Nov 2015 and rejected it in Dec 2015 due to lack of credibility on central elements.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD erred in assessing her religious identity, documentary evidence, and credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its assessment of her religious identity, treatment of her supporting documentary evidence and in assessing her credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in assessing her religious identity, evidence, and credibility.

propositions.text: Huruglica guides the RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal reviewing all aspects and substituting its own decision if it departs from the RPD.
propositions.quote: Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision.

propositions.text: The RAD can respect RPD credibility findings but is not restricted to intervening only for overriding and palpable errors.
propositions.quote: [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Huruglica requires the RAD to conduct a hybrid appeal, independently assessing and substituting decisions, respecting RPD credibility findings but not limited to palpable errors.

propositions.text: The RAD will independently assess the RPD decision and afford deference to RPD credibility findings or where RPD has advantage.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will independently assess the RPD decision, giving deference to RPD credibility findings or where it has an advantage.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant's ability to exit China on her own passport undermined her claim and drew an adverse credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the Appellant's ability to exit China on her own passport at a time she alleges she was wanted by the Public Security Bureau (PSB).

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant exited China on her own identity document, undermining her allegation of being wanted by police.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant exited China on her own identity document, thus undermining her allegation that she was wanted by the police.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's exit on her own passport undermined her claim and credibility.

propositions.text: The RAD finds documentary evidence that China has the Golden Shield Project, a national policing database with extensive tracking technology.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the documentary evidence reveals that the Chinese government has a national computer network known as the Golden Shield Project, and the PSB has access to a national policing database, which includes information about criminal fugitives and information on passports and exit and entry. The Golden Shield incorporated extensive tracking and control mechanisms including facial recognition surveillance technology.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds evidence that China has the Golden Shield Project, a national policing database with extensive tracking technology.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the Exit and Entry Administration Law of China restricts exit for suspects and requires formal procedures for preventing exit.
propositions.quote: The RAD also notes from its own review and assessment of the evidence that the Exit and Entry Administration Law of China, which came into force on 1 July 2013, states the following:...

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes China's Exit and Entry Law restricts exit for suspects and requires formal procedures to prevent exit.

propositions.text: The RAD acknowledges evidence that airport security officials access the PSB's online database to track and detain wanted persons.
propositions.quote: The panel also acknowledges that the documentation states that security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities...

paragraphs.summary: The RAD acknowledges evidence that airport security officials access the PSB database to track and detain wanted persons.

propositions.text: An article states all police units have access to eight public security databases including population, border exit and entry, and criminal investigations.
propositions.quote: An undated article on the website of the Ministry of Public Security, entitled: "Deepening the Implementation of the 'Golden Shield' Project" states that: ... all police units nationwide have access to eight public security databases, including the "National Basic Population Information Database"...

paragraphs.summary: An article states all police units have access to multiple public security databases including border exit and entry.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the system has been used to track down cult practitioners, including Falun Gong.
propositions.quote: In particular, the RAD notes that the system has been used to track down cult practitioners. The Chinese economist writing in Open Magazine affirms that: ...Cisco's Policenet has been helping the [Chinese Communist Party]'s public security organs to ferret out political dissidents and Falun Gong practitioners for years.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the system tracks cult practitioners and political dissidents like Falun Gong.

propositions.text: The Golden Shield incorporates tracking mechanisms like real-name registration, GPS, and facial recognition to identify disruptive individuals.
propositions.quote: In addition, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation provided the following information: [T]he Golden Shield incorporates extensive tracking and control mechanisms such as real-name online registration requirements, GPS monitoring, and facial recognition surveillance technology in a multi-pronged approach to identify potentially disruptive individuals.

paragraphs.summary: The Golden Shield uses tracking mechanisms like real-name registration, GPS, and facial recognition to identify disruptive individuals.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD's finding is unreasonable for not explaining why she couldn't exit with a smuggler's bribery despite the Golden Shield evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD's finding is unreasonable because the RPD's reasons do not explain why the Golden Shield project or the documentary evidence relied upon by the RPD leads to the conclusions that she would not be able to exit with the assistance of a smuggler who bribed officials.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits the RPD ignored relevant case law (Sun) decided on similar facts and evidence of China's policing expertise.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also submits that the RPD ignores relevant case law (Sun) which was decided on similar facts and in the face of the same evidence of China's policing expertise.

propositions.text: The Appellant submits Sun's facts cannot be distinguished as it was decided in March 2015.
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the facts in Sun cannot be distinguished from the facts in the present case because Sun was determined on March 27, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD's finding is unreasonable for ignoring bribery possibility and relevant case law Sun decided on similar facts.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the RPD's analysis of exit on own passport could be more fulsome but RAD must conduct its own evidence analysis.
propositions.quote: While it is true that the RPD's analysis of the Appellant's ability to exit China using her own passport could have been more fulsome, the RAD finds that the jurisprudence requires the RAD to conduct its own analysis of the evidence in the record.

propositions.text: The RAD reviews and assesses the evidence and notes Sun was decided relative to an RPD decision based on 2012 evidence.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD reviews and assesses the evidence and comes to its own conclusions on the Appellant's exit from China. The RAD notes that while it is true that the Federal Court decision in Sun was determined in March 2015, it was relative to a decision of the RPD that was made in November 2013.

propositions.text: Sun referenced the RPD's reliance on a 2012 National Documentation Package and noted challenges in police information sharing.
propositions.quote: In the Sun matter, the reviewing court made reference to the RPD's reliance on an Information Request reporting the existence and expansion of a national Chinese policing database used by the PSB and at ports of entry and exit of the country and that the same document also mentions that challenges remain with respect to information sharing between regional police units.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds RPD's analysis could be fuller but conducts its own review, noting Sun was based on older evidence and police info sharing challenges.

propositions.text: The RAD notes the most current evidence confirms airport officials access the PSB database and coordinate with police to track and detain wanted persons.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes, however, the conclusions drawn about the plausibility of the Appellant being able to leave China on her own passport is based on the most current information in the NDP. The RAD notes that in 10 February 2014 correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Executive Director of the Dui Hua Foundation affirmed that airport security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities [also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield] and that there is concrete evidence of airport officials coordinating with police departments in tracking and detaining wanted persons.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes current evidence confirms airport officials access the PSB database and coordinate to track and detain wanted persons.

propositions.text: The RAD finds China's security practices have become more stringent with multiple systems to identify persons leaving the country.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes, from its analysis of the Golden Shield, that it is clear that the security practices have become increasingly stringent in recent years in China and that there a number of systems now in place to identify persons leaving the country.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds China's security practices have become more stringent with multiple systems to identify persons leaving.

propositions.text: The Appellant relies on Federal Court decision Ren to argue RPD's finding is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Appellant relies on the more recent Federal Court decision in Ren to support her argument that the RPD's finding is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The RAD notes Ren involved a passport not scanned, but no evidence here shows the Appellant's passport was not scanned; it bears an exit stamp.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the facts in Ren are that the passport was not scanned. However, there is no evidence offered by the Appellant in the present case which establishes that her passport was not scanned by officials. Furthermore, the RAD notes that the Appellant's passport bears an exit stamp indicating that it was examined.

propositions.text: The Appellant relies on Federal Court decision Zhang to argue bribing one official could allow exit without difficulty.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also relies on the Federal Court decision in Zhang to argue that it is plausible that bribing "one person with a computer would be sufficient" to allow the Appellant to exit China without difficulty.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the suggestion that one bribe could remove police interest from the Golden Shield system is implausible.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the suggestion implies that one bribe could facilitate the removal of police interest in the Appellant from the Golden Shield computer system.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant relies on Ren and Zhang cases to argue bribery could allow exit; the RAD finds no evidence passport was unscanned and one bribe removing police interest is implausible.

propositions.text: The RAD finds it illogical that a smuggler would accompany the Appellant through airport if bribery removed police interest.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellant alleges that the smuggler accompanied her throughout her travel from China to Toronto. If the smuggler was able to bribe an official to alter computerized records of the police interest in the Appellant, the RAD finds it makes little sense that the smuggler would place himself at risk by accompanying the Appellant through the airport and onto the aircraft when there was no need.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the Golden Shield is extensive and likely has redundant systems preventing compromise by a single individual.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the RAD finds that evidence reveals that the Golden Shield system is an extensive security apparatus that is far-reaching and encompassing. The RAD finds that given the importance of this system to Chinese authorities in monitoring its citizens, it is reasonable to expect that the use of the apparatus is also monitored and that there are redundant systems in place to prevent the system from being compromised by a single individual.

propositions.text: The Appellant's allegation that PSB pursued her after departure undermines the bribery theory removing police interest from the system.
propositions.quote: In addition, the RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that the PSB have continued to pursue her after her departure from China. The RAD finds that this allegation undermines the suggestion that a smuggler was able to remove police interest in the Appellant from the Golden Shield system.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds it illogical a smuggler would accompany the Appellant if bribery removed police interest; the Golden Shield is extensive with redundancies; PSB pursuit after departure undermines bribery theory.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified her passport was examined four times during travel.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified that her passport was examined four different times during her travel

propositions.text: Article 51 requires companies transporting goods and passengers to declare information before departure or entry.
propositions.quote: Article 51 of the Exit and Entry Administration Law of the People's Republic of China require that companies involved in the transportation of goods and passengers in and out of Chinese ports must declare information on the goods and passengers in advance of their departure or entry to the country

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant's passport was examined four times and Article 51 requires transport companies to declare passenger info before departure or entry.

propositions.text: It is highly improbable the smuggler knew who to bribe at each checkpoint.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it highly improbable that the smuggler would have the prior knowledge of who to bribe in order to facilitate safe travel through each checkpoint

propositions.text: Local authorities likely entered the Appellant's info into a database to apprehend her.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to expect that the local authorities would have entered her information into the database to further their efforts to apprehend her

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds it improbable the smuggler knew who to bribe and local authorities likely entered the Appellant's info into a database.

propositions.text: Some smugglers may have customs official connections to bypass security.
propositions.quote: it may be possible that some smugglers may have connections with specific customs officials to circumvent security at some Chinese airports

propositions.text: Smuggling is high risk; smugglers protect collaborators and would not return passports that could be traced back.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to expect that smugglers do everything possible to protect their illicit enterprises which would include protecting their collaborators at Chinese airports... it is reasonable to expect that the smuggler would not return the passport to the Appellant in the event it could be traced back to him or his customs control collaborator

propositions.text: Given the fraudulent visa, bribery, and exit stamp, the Appellant's testimony is neither plausible nor credible.
propositions.quote: Given the smuggler is alleged to have obtained the visa fraudulently, and bribed specific border control officer and that the Appellant's passport bears an exit stamp, it is reasonable to expect that the smuggler would not return the passport to the Appellant... the RAD finds the Appellant's testimony neither plausible nor credible

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds smuggling is risky, smugglers protect collaborators, and the Appellant's testimony about passport return is not credible.

propositions.text: There is evidence of corruption in China but insufficient evidence it extends to airport security.
propositions.quote: there is no mention in the paper and insufficient evidence elsewhere... that establishes that corruption extends to the airport security apparatus

propositions.text: Corruption is concentrated in sectors with extensive state involvement, not airport security.
propositions.quote: corruption problems are concentrated in sectors with extensive state involvement, such as construction, land use, infrastructure, property development and banking

propositions.text: Former Premier Wen Jiabao said corruption occurs in departments with great power and centralized fund management.
propositions.quote: Former Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said in March 2012 that corruption tends to occur frequently in departments that possess great power and in areas where the management of funds is centralised

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes corruption exists in China but not shown to extend to airport security, citing Wen Jiabao's statement on corruption.

propositions.text: Objective evidence on Golden Shield and border controls is compelling and convincing.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the objective evidence concerning the Golden Shield and other border controls in place in China is compelling and convincing

propositions.text: It is highly unlikely the Appellant bypassed all security controls in China.
propositions.quote: it is highly unlikely that the Appellant could have bypassed all of the security controls in place

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the evidence on border controls compelling and that it is highly unlikely the Appellant bypassed all security controls.

propositions.text: RPD may reject evidence inconsistent with probabilities and make findings based on implausibility, common sense, and rationality.
propositions.quote: the RPD is entitled to make reasonable findings based on implausibility, common sense and rationality, and it may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole

propositions.text: Credibility findings based on plausibility require evidential foundation.
propositions.quote: Where the panel finds a lack of credibility based on inferences concerning the plausibility of evidence, there must be a basis in the evidence to support such inferences

propositions.text: In this case, there is evidential foundation for the panel's findings.
propositions.quote: In this case, there is an evidential foundation for the panel's findings

paragraphs.summary: The RAD states RPD can reject evidence inconsistent with probabilities and has evidential foundation for its findings here.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with RPD that it is not credible or plausible the Appellant left China on her own passport after PSB attention.
propositions.quote: the RAD agrees with the RPD's findings and does not find it credible or plausible that the Appellant was able to leave China on her own passport after coming to the attention of the PSB

propositions.text: The RAD draws a negative inference about the truth of the Appellant's allegations of PSB pursuit due to Christian activities.
propositions.quote: draws a negative inference as it relates to the XXXX of her allegations that she was being pursued by the PSB because of her Christian XXXX activities

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD that the Appellant's claim of leaving China on her own passport is not credible and draws a negative inference on her PSB pursuit claim.

propositions.text: The RPD's adverse credibility finding about PSB visits to family is unclear and speculative about PSB beliefs.
propositions.quote: the Appellant submits that the RPD's finding in this regard is unclear... it is impossible to speculate on what the PSB believed and that the RPD cannot put itself in the mind of a foreign police service

propositions.text: Monthly PSB visits to family are plausible and consistent with documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: there is nothing implausible or incredible about the fact that the PSB attended her home once per month and that it is in keeping with the documentary evidence

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD's adverse credibility finding on PSB family visits is unclear, speculative, and monthly visits are plausible.

propositions.text: The RPD's adverse credibility finding concerns the family's ability to live normally despite PSB interest in the Appellant.
propositions.quote: the RPD's finding in this regard is in relation to the treatment of the Appellant's family in China... adverse credibility finding based on the ability of the Appellant's family in China to carry on with their lives without facing serious consequences

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the RPD's adverse credibility finding relates to the family's normal life despite PSB interest in the Appellant.

propositions.text: The Appellant testified family faced no significant consequences beyond questioning about her whereabouts.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified that her family in China did not face any significant consequences beyond being questioned about the whereabouts of the Appellant

propositions.text: This lack of consequences is inconsistent with the objective evidence.
propositions.quote: the fact that the Appellant's family did not face any consequences for the Appellant's actions is inconsistent with the objective evidence in the record

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the Appellant's family faced no significant consequences, inconsistent with objective evidence.

propositions.text: The XXXX sect is banned and identified as an 'evil cult' in China.
propositions.quote: the evidence in the record establishes that the XXXX sect of Christianity is a banned religion in China and is identified, along with other religions such as Falun Gong, as an "evil cult"

propositions.text: Family members of XXXX sect practitioners are reasonably expected to be treated like Falun Gong family members.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to expect that family members of the XXXX practitioners would be treated similarly to family members of Falun Gong practitioners

propositions.text: Country evidence shows Falun Gong family members face persecution including loss of employment and torture.
propositions.quote: family members can face consequences solely because one member of their family in engaged in Falun Gong activities... ranging from loss of employment to torture

propositions.text: Falun Gong family members suffer mistreatment including detention and torture.
propositions.quote: some family members of practitioners have suffered the "same mistreatments as practitioners" themselves, including detention and torture

propositions.text: Persecution includes pressuring spouses to divorce, threatening careers, expelling children, and orphaning children.
propositions.quote: pressuring spouses to divorce, threatening to end the careers of relatives, expelling the children of active Falun Gong members from school, and leaving some children orphaned or alone due to the detention or execution of one or both of their parents

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes the XXXX sect is banned and family members face persecution similar to Falun Gong families, including severe mistreatment.

propositions.text: A 2008 report still accurately describes persecution of Falun Gong family members, with improved targeting by Public Security database.
propositions.quote: the 2008 report still accurately describes the treatment of family members and relatives of Falun Gong practitioners... except "that the Public Security database has improved, allowing them to be more precise in who they target and in carrying out the persecution"

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes a 2008 report still accurately describes Falun Gong family persecution with improved targeting by Public Security.

propositions.text: PSB may not pursue families in every case but here it is reasonable to expect family faced greater sanctions to pressure Appellant.
propositions.quote: it is reasonable to expect that her family would have experienced some greater sanctions in an effort to have the Appellant turn herself into the PSB

propositions.text: Appellant testified family lived normally without sanctions despite PSB visits.
propositions.quote: the Appellant has testified that her family have been able to carry on their lives normally and have not experienced any other sanctions

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with RPD that continued PSB visits without increased coercion makes little sense.
propositions.quote: The RAD agrees with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony that her family continued to receive these visits even though they knew she was not there makes little sense without an increase in the coercive measures applied by the PSB

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds it reasonable family faced sanctions but Appellant testified family lived normally; continued PSB visits without coercion is implausible.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the Appellant is not wanted by the PSB in China.
propositions.quote: the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not wanted by the PSB in China

paragraphs.summary: The RAD concludes on balance of probabilities the Appellant is not wanted by the PSB in China.

propositions.text: RPD drew adverse credibility finding on family register (hukou) because brother's info was missing despite testimony he lived at same address.
propositions.quote: The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the fact that despite the Appellant's testimony that her brother resided at the same address as her, the hukou did not include her brother's information

propositions.text: RPD rejected Appellant's explanation that brother's hukou was removed after joining army.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation that her brother's hukou had been removed by Chinese officials after her brother joined the army

propositions.text: RPD reasoned documentary evidence does not support pages being removed from hukou and brother's page should have PSB notations.
propositions.quote: The RPD reasoned that the documentary evidence does not support the notion that pages can be taken out of the hukou and that her brother's page should have been included in the hukou but with notations from the PSB to indicate the change

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found adverse credibility on the hukou because brother's info was missing and rejected explanation of transfer to military hukou.

propositions.text: RPD misconstrued evidence; brother's hukou transferred after joining army in 2012.
propositions.quote: the Appellant argues that the RPD misconstrued her evidence and that her testimony was that his hukou had been transferred out after he joined the army in 2012

propositions.text: Documentary evidence supports brother's transfer to military hukou after joining army.
propositions.quote: documentary evidence supports that her brother would have been transferred to a military hukou from the family hukou after he joined the army

propositions.text: Hukou issued in 2014 after brother joined army, so plausible he was transferred out and not included.
propositions.quote: the hukou was issued in XXXX 2014 after the Appellant's brother joined the army and as such it is plausible that he would have been transferred out to a military hukou and would not have been included in the 2014 hukou

propositions.text: RPD's finding that omission was 'notable' is unreasonable and irrelevant to central claim elements.
propositions.quote: this finding in not relevant to the central elements of the claim

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD misconstrued evidence; brother's hukou transferred after army enlistment and omission is irrelevant to claim.

propositions.text: The RAD finds the RPD misstated the Appellant's testimony about brother's residence and finds explanation consistent with evidence.
propositions.quote: the RAD finds that the RPD did misstate the Appellant's testimony... the Appellant's explanation is consistent with the documentary evidence with regard to her younger brother's transfer to a military hukou

propositions.text: The RPD's question could have been interpreted as past tense regarding who lived at the address.
propositions.quote: the manner in which the question was put to her by the RPD could easily have been interpreted as past tense

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds RPD misstated testimony and Appellant's explanation about brother's military hukou transfer is consistent with evidence.

propositions.text: Before 2012, brother lived at the address; Appellant's response was accurate.
propositions.quote: prior to 2012, the Appellant's younger brother had lived at that address and in this regard the Appellant's response was accurate

propositions.text: Without further questioning, RPD's conclusion that Appellant referred to present time is not supportable.
propositions.quote: in the absence of any further questioning of the Appellant on this issue, the RPD's conclusion that the Appellant was referring to the present time is not supportable

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds brother lived at address before 2012 and RPD's conclusion about present tense is unsupported without further questioning.

propositions.text: RPD's finding is based on microscopic examination and omission is not central or material to persecution allegations.
propositions.quote: the RPD's finding is based on a microscopic examination of the evidence and that the omission at issue is not central or key to the Appellant's allegations of persecution and that it has no materiality to her allegations of actual persecution and cannot be sustained

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds RPD's adverse finding on omission is microscopic, not central, and has no materiality to persecution allegations.

propositions.text: RPD erred by failing to consider summons and Notice of Dismissal tendered by Appellant.
propositions.quote: the Appellant submits that the RPD erred by failing to consider the summons and Notice of Dismissal she tendered in support of her allegations

propositions.text: Failure to address significant documents renders RPD decision unsustainable.
propositions.quote: a failure to do so renders the RPD decision unsustainable

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD erred by not considering summons and dismissal notice, making the decision unsustainable.

propositions.text: RPD did not analyze or provide reasons for rejecting documents, but RAD finds documents cannot be relied upon after its own review
propositions.quote: While it is problematic that the RPD did not conduct an analysis of/or provide reasons for rejecting these documents, the RAD finds, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, that there are sufficient grounds for the RAD to find that the documents cannot be relied upon.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the documents cannot be relied upon despite RPD's lack of analysis, after its own review.

propositions.text: Summons tendered is a non-coercive investigative summons under Article 82 PSAPL requiring appearance for interrogation
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that summons tendered by the Appellant is a non-coercive investigative summons issued under the authority of the Article 82 of the Public Security and Administrative Punishment Law of the People's Republic of China (PSAPL) and which required the Appellant to appear for interrogation.

propositions.text: Article 82 states evading a summons can lead to a compulsory summons
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that Article 82 specifically states that anyone who evades a summons can result in a compulsory summons.

propositions.text: Appellant has not tendered a coercive summons
propositions.quote: The RAD notes, however, that the Appellant has not tendered a coercive summons.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the summons is non-coercive under Article 82 PSAPL, evading summons can lead to compulsory summons, but no coercive summons was tendered.

propositions.text: Chinese authorities view adherents of XXXX faith as cult members
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that, given that the Chinese authorities view adherents of the XXXX faith as members of a cult.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows XXXX Christianity is banned and identified as an 'evil cult' in China
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the documentary evidence in the record indicates that XXXX sect of Christianity is a banned religion in China and is identified, along with other certain other religions, as an "evil cult."

propositions.text: Evil cults are subject to severe treatment and pursued by extra-judicial 6-10 Office
propositions.quote: Furthermore, religions deemed as evil cults are subject to the most severe treatment of all, and are pursued by an extra-judicial law enforcement branch known as the 6-10 Office.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Chinese authorities view XXXX faith as a banned evil cult pursued severely by the 6-10 Office.

propositions.text: Family members of evil cult practitioners often face arbitrary imprisonment and harassment
propositions.quote: There is evidence in the national documentation that family members of "evil cult" practitioners are likewise often subject to arbitrary imprisonment and harassment.

propositions.text: Authorities pressure family members to force accused into compliance
propositions.quote: and are often pressured by authorities to force the accused into compliance or submission.

propositions.text: Given evidence and appellant's allegations, reasonable to expect coercive summons if appellant failed to report
propositions.quote: In light of the objective evidence regarding the vigorous efforts the authorities undertake to pursue members of the faith, and the Appellant allegations of the arrest of co-practitioners and ongoing visits to her family home as well as the allegation that the PSB informed the Appellant's employer, it is reasonable to expect that a coercive summons would have been issued when the Appellant failed to report for the interview.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds family members face harassment and expects coercive summons given appellant's allegations and authorities' efforts.

propositions.text: Appellant testified family notified her about non-coercive summons
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that in light of the fact that the Appellant has testified that her family notified her about the issuance of the non-coercive summons.

propositions.text: If coercive summons had been issued, appellant would have been notified by family
propositions.quote: it is also reasonable to expect that if a coercive summons had been issued for the Appellant, she would have been notified by her family.

propositions.text: Absence of compulsory summons when expected undermines genuineness of tendered summons
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the absence of a compulsory summons when it reasonable to expect that the Appellant would have been issued such a summons undermines the genuineness of the summons she did tender.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds absence of compulsory summons undermines genuineness of tendered summons given family notification testimony.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states PSB summons can be oral or written and issued only after case filed
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the RAD notes that the documentary evidence states that the PSB summons can be oral or written and can be issued only after a case has been filed for investigation.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes PSB summons can be oral or written and issued only after investigation case is filed.

propositions.text: Public security summonses cannot last more than 12 or 24 hours depending on violation
propositions.quote: Regardless of the form they take, public security summonses cannot last more than twelve hours, or twenty-four hours if the person is suspected of administrative violations punishable by detention.

propositions.text: Appellant alleges PSB attended home to arrest her and co-practitioners were arrested
propositions.quote: However, the Appellant has alleged that the PSB attended her home in an effort to arrest her. In addition, she alleges that two of her co-practitioners were arrested by the PSB.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes summons duration limits and appellant's allegations of PSB arrest attempts and co-practitioner arrests.

propositions.text: Alleged PSB actions inconsistent with use of public security summons
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the alleged actions of the PSB and the arrest and detention of co-practitioners is inconsistent with the use of a public security summons.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence states coercive summons and arrest warrants can be used by PSB
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the documentary evidence states that coercive summons and arrest warrants are instruments that can be used by the PSB.

propositions.text: Given PSB's use of 6-10 Office and arrest allegations, reasonable to expect coercive instruments rather than investigative summons
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that, in light of the documentary evidence, the police employs the use of the extra-judicial law enforcement branch known as the 6-10 Office to investigate cult religions, it is reasonable to expect that, given the allegations of the PSB's efforts to arrest the Appellant and their arrest of the Appellant's co-practitioners, if the PSB were going to employ the use of a summons would employ the use of these coercive instruments to carry out their intention to arrest the Appellant, rather than employ the use of an investigative instrument.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds PSB's alleged arrests inconsistent with summons use and expects coercive instruments given 6-10 Office involvement.

propositions.text: PSAPL penalties for cult participation cannot exceed 15 days
propositions.quote: The Public Security and Administrative Punishment Law states that penalties resulting from enforcement under the provisions of the PSAPL in relation to participation in the practice of cults cannot exceed 15 days.

propositions.text: This is inconsistent with appellant's allegation that co-practitioners remain detained
propositions.quote: which is inconsistent with her allegations that the co-practitioners who were arrested are still in detention.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes PSAPL penalties max 15 days, inconsistent with co-practitioners' alleged ongoing detention.

propositions.text: Appellant's allegations and testimony inconsistent with objective evidence on PSAPL provisions
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant's allegations and testimony are inconsistent with the objective evidence in the record with regard to the provisions of the PSAPL.

propositions.text: Little weight can be given to the summons in establishing appellant is pursued by PSB
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on the basis of the foregoing, little weight can be given to this summons in establishing that the Appellant is being pursued by the PSB.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant's allegations inconsistent with evidence and gives little weight to the summons for PSB pursuit claim.

propositions.text: RPD failed to assess all critical corroborative documents, especially letter of dismissal from employer
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to assess all of the critical corroborative documents that she submitted to substantiate her claim. In particular, the Appellant argues that the RPD failed to assess the letter of dismissal from her employer in China which states that she was dismissed from her job because her employer was informed by the PSB of her illegal and evil religious activities.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD failed to assess critical documents, especially the dismissal letter from her employer.

propositions.text: RPD did not analyze Notice of Dismissal but RAD can conduct own analysis
propositions.quote: While it is problematic that the RPD did not appear to conduct any analysis of the Notice of Dismissal, the RAD finds that it can conduct its own analysis and come to its own conclusions.

propositions.text: Little weight given to letter of dismissal as it is a simple computer-generated document without signature
propositions.quote: The RAD finds little weight can be given to this document. First, the RAD's assessment of the letter of dismissal reveals it is a simple computer generated document that could be created by anyone with a simple word processing program. The RAD also notes that, although the letter has an ink stamp, the letter lacks a signature.

propositions.text: Document does not overcome adverse credibility findings or establish appellant as genuine XXXX Christian
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that this document does not overcome the significant adverse credibility findings of the RAD and does not establish that the Appellant is a genuine XXXX Christian.

propositions.text: Appellant alleged using fraudulently obtained visa to travel to Canada, showing ability and willingness to use fraudulent documents
propositions.quote: Secondly, the Appellant has alleged that she used a fraudulently obtained visa to travel to Canada. In doing so, she has acknowledged that she has the ability to acquire and willingness to use fraudulent documents.

propositions.text: Adverse credibility findings undermine appellant's allegations of PSB pursuit for religious reasons
propositions.quote: Thirdly, the RAD notes that the totality of the adverse credibility findings undermines her allegations that she is being pursued by the PSB because she is a XXXX or for any other reason.

propositions.text: Prevalence of fraudulent documents in China noted
propositions.quote: Finally, the RAD notes the prevalence of fraudulent documents in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the dismissal letter unreliable and undermined by appellant's adverse credibility and fraud allegations.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding appellant not genuine practitioner despite correct answers about faith
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it found that she was not a genuine practitioner despite her ability to correctly answer questions put to her about practice of the faith.

propositions.text: Insufficient reason to reject her allegation of being a XXXX faith practitioner
propositions.quote: She argues there is insufficient reason to reject her allegation that she is a practitioner of the XXXX faith.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred in rejecting her as a genuine practitioner despite her correct faith knowledge.

propositions.text: RAD not persuaded by appellant's argument and finds allegations not credible on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard. The RAD finds, on the basis of the foregoing findings and on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegations that she was a practitioner of the XXXX sect in China are not credible.

propositions.text: Appellant has some knowledge of Christianity but may have gained it in Canada after arrival
propositions.quote: While it is true that she has some knowledge of Christianity, the RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that she had been attending a church since her arrival in Canada. As such, the knowledge she possesses could easily have been gained in Canada.

propositions.text: Basic knowledge of faith does not necessarily reflect genuine or false practice
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that merely having some information regarding basic teachings and practice or the lack of such information does not necessarily reflect genuine or false practice.

propositions.text: Little weight given to appellant's ability to answer questions about XXXX Christians
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that little weight can be given to the Appellant's ability to answer questions about XXXX Christians.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant's allegations not credible, knowledge possibly gained in Canada, and little weight to her faith knowledge.

propositions.text: Correct answers do not overcome serious credibility findings
propositions.quote: Furthermore, even though the Appellant was able to correctly answer some questions put to her about Christianity, the RAD finds those correct responses could not overcome the serious credibility findings.

propositions.text: Appellant failed to provide sufficient reliable evidence to establish genuine XXXX membership on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that, given the serious credibility finding, the Appellant has failed to provide sufficient reliable evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that she was a genuine XXXX in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant's correct answers insufficient to overcome credibility issues and fails to prove genuine membership.

propositions.text: On totality of adverse findings, RAD finds appellant not genuine XXXX member and not pursued by PSB
propositions.quote: On the basis of the totality of the adverse findings, the RAD finds, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, that the Appellant is not a genuine member of the XXXX Christian sect and that she is not being pursued by the PSB.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant not a genuine XXXX member and not pursued by PSB based on total adverse findings.

propositions.text: Difficult to judge genuineness of religious practice but RAD finds appellant not genuine practicing Christian
propositions.quote: The RAD acknowledges that it is difficult to make a judgement regarding the genuineness of a person's religious practice. However, on the basis of a full assessment of the evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellant is not a genuine practicing Christian, and that these credibility findings raise a significant doubt about her general credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant's knowledge of XXXX sect likely obtained in Canada to support fraudulent claim
propositions.quote: Having found that the Appellant is not a practicing XXXX Christian, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of findings noted above, that whatever knowledge of the XXXX sect of Christianity the Appellant possesses was obtained in Canada for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim.

propositions.text: Appellant is not a genuine practicing XXXX Christian or any other Christian denomination
propositions.quote: In the context as noted above, and on the basis of the totality of evidence disclosed and in the context of the Appellant's knowledge of XXXX sect Christian teachings, the RAD therefore finds that the Appellant is not a genuine practicing XXXX Christian or a Christian of any other denomination.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds appellant not a genuine practicing Christian; her knowledge likely gained in Canada to support fraudulent claim.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with RPD that appellant is not a genuine Christian on balance of probabilities
propositions.quote: Having reviewed all the evidence in this appeal, the RAD agrees with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not a genuine Christian.

propositions.text: RAD agrees with RPD that appellant is not wanted by Chinese authorities for XXXX Christian activities or any other reason
propositions.quote: The RAD further agrees with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not wanted by the authorities in China because of XXXX Christian activities or for any other reason.

propositions.text: Appellant has not satisfied burden to establish serious possibility of persecution or personal risk
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not satisfied her burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with RPD that appellant is not genuine Christian, not wanted by authorities, and fails to prove persecution risk.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(a), RAD confirms RPD decision and dismisses appeal
propositions.quote: Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA s.111(1)(a).
